extracted.intended_audience: researchers at any level (graduate students, postdocs, junior and senior faculty) who want to understand or participate in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A general, practical guide explaining how the scientific peer review process works, how reviewers are selected and motivated, common review formats (single-/double-blind/open), typical reviewer requests, criticisms of the system, and ways authors/reviewers can engage (including preprint commenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript quality criteria (what peer review checks for)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review evaluates academic work before publication to ensure that published research is original, impactful, and performed according to the standard best practices of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a filter, fact-checker, and redundancy-detector; its goal is to legitimize research, bolster researchers by improving manuscripts, and give science credibility compared with non–peer-reviewed outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial pre-screening requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts often must pass multiple steps of pre-screening by journal editors before entering formal peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Getting a manuscript peer reviewed is a privilege; editorial checks can block many submissions prior to reviewer assignment (the page references a process diagram summarizing this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be well versed in the subject matter; criteria for 'well versed' differ between journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-impact journals may check a potential reviewer's publication history, recency of publications, and the impact factor of journals where they published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reviewer selection methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are selected in several common ways: by the journal editor; suggested by the researchers; selected from the journal’s editorial board; or suggested by reviewers who decline an invitation to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding subject-matter experts is difficult because reviewing is voluntary and potential reviewers are often busy with their own research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer compensation and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers are typically unpaid (pro bono), and reviewing is not a paid job among scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-monetary benefits include reciprocity (expectation others will review your work), prestige/tenure recognition (reviews on CVs; invitations to editorships), early access to novel research, and improved critical thinking skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: In single-blind review, reviewers know the researchers’ identities but the researchers do not know who the reviewers are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most common type in academic research; it protects reviewer anonymity while exposing potential author identity bias to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: In double-blind review, both the authors’ and reviewers’ identities are protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page calls this 'the freest of bias' because it reduces identity-based bias, though operational challenges (deducing authors) remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: In open peer review everyone knows who everyone is; authors know their reviewers and reviewers know the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals publish reviewers’ names and comments with the article (BMJ, EMBO Journal, European Journal of Neuroscience). Proponents say it yields better, more thorough, and more courteous reviews; downsides include increased risk of bias and quid pro quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint/crowdsourced peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Public commentary on preprints is a form of peer review where peers provide open feedback before formal journal review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprint commentary gives authors quick, broad feedback they can use to improve manuscripts before formal submission; it is essentially crowdsourcing of peer review and often precedes traditional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness (speed of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slow feedback is a common criticism: the time between submission and publication can take months or years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow turnaround times are demoralizing and particularly harmful for graduate students, postdocs, and junior faculty on time-sensitive career timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is subject to human biases: reviewers may be dogmatic, favor well-known scientists, or otherwise evaluate non-objectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open review can exacerbate some biases; editors and systems must account for reputation effects and individual reviewer prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias from author-suggested reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors suggesting reviewers can introduce bias because they may be inclined to propose people who will view their work favorably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should vet suggested reviewers for conflicts and closeness to authors to avoid biased selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest / 'too close' reviewer exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested reviewers who are 'too close' to the authors (e.g., at the same institute or frequent coauthors) may be rejected due to conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors commonly screen for conflicts and avoid assigning reviewers with close institutional or collaborative ties to the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum number of reviewers and resolving divergent reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals usually choose a minimum of two reviewers and may use a third reviewer if the two reviews are wildly different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice helps compensate for occasional low reviewer expertise and reduces the impact of an outlier review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical reviewer feedback content (what reviewers request)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers commonly request actions such as repeating experiments, providing raw data, performing additional experiments, including new figures, and fixing grammatical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such requests aim to improve the rigor, reproducibility, clarity, and presentation of the manuscript; authors often become stronger researchers as a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low reviewer expertise as a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reviewing is unpaid and relies on goodwill, journals may sometimes get reviewers with insufficient expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as a key challenge; editors mitigate it by selecting multiple reviewers and by rejecting reviewers deemed too close or insufficiently expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for broader participation and future improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review’s major challenges include bias, finding expert reviewers, slowness, and debates about compensation; improvements include experimenting with diverse methods of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends more scientists at all levels participate in reviewing as one way to improve the system and lists newer, diverse review methods (e.g., open review, preprint commentary) as part of the future.
